overview.text: Duke Power Company has applied for a license to build the 1,000-MW Bad Creek Pumped Storage Project No. 2740 in Oconee County, South Carolina, using a new 318-acre upper reservoir on Bad and West Bad Creeks and the existing 7,565-acre Lake Jocassee as the lower reservoir. The project is in a remote, rugged four-county region (Oconee and Pickens in SC; Jackson and Transylvania in NC) dominated by textiles and wood products, with no residences requiring relocation. Alternatives evaluated include other pumped storage sites (Long Spur Ridge, Bearcamp Creek, Coley Creek), conventional hydro, combustion turbines, coal-fired and nuclear generation, conservation/rate revision, purchase of power, and denial of the application. Major environmental impacts include clearing about 505 acres, eliminating roughly 2.3 miles of trout stream, reducing flow in Howard Creek, and possibly reducing coldwater trout habitat in Lake Jocassee. Public response was mixed: the Mayor of Walhalla and the Nuclear Regulatory Commission were favorable, while the South Carolina Wildlife and Marine Resources Department, Trout Unlimited, and the Sierra Club opposed or raised serious reservations, and EPA gave an ER-2 rating.

project_description.text: Duke Power Company seeks a license for the 1,000-MW Bad Creek Pumped Storage Project No. 2740 on Bad and West Bad Creeks in Oconee County, South Carolina. The project would include a 318-acre upper reservoir, a 1.25-mile-long underground power tunnel, and an underground powerhouse with four 250-MW reversible pump-turbine units, discharging into the existing 7,565-acre Lake Jocassee as the lower reservoir. A 525-kV transmission line approximately 18 miles long would connect the project to the Oconee Nuclear Station switchyard, with pumping energy supplied largely from Duke's Oconee Nuclear Plant. The project would be capable of operating continuously at full load for 32 hours.

A 525-kV transmission line would run from the Bad Creek Project area to the Oconee Nuclear Station switchyard via new and existing rights-of-way.

affected_community.text: The project lies in Oconee County, South Carolina, about 8 miles north-northwest of Salem and 35 miles west-northwest of Greenville, in a rugged, remote area where no residences or businesses would need to be relocated. The surrounding four-county area (Oconee and Pickens in SC; Jackson and Transylvania in NC) had a 1970 population of 140,990 and is dominated by textile and wood-products manufacturing. Required project lands are held by Crescent Land and Timber Corporation, a wholly owned Duke Power subsidiary, and the project would generate approximately $950,000 annually in tax revenue to Oconee County, with about 100 new construction-worker families expected to relocate to the area.

alternatives_overview.text: Alternatives considered include denial of the application, alternative pumped storage sites (Long Spur Ridge, Bearcamp Creek, and Coley Creek), alternative generation methods (conventional hydro, simple- and combined-cycle combustion turbines, coal-fired steam cycling, base-load nuclear), conservation and rate revision, purchase of power, and federal development. Of 24 alternative pumped storage sites identified by the Applicant, the five most desirable were selected for further consideration. With the possible exception of Long Spur Ridge, Bad Creek is the lowest-cost power source available to the Applicant, with estimated annual savings of approximately $38,700,000 by 1990. Conservation, rate revision, and power purchase were determined not to be reasonable alternatives at this time, and without the project Duke's reserve margins beyond 1982 would fall below the 18-22% recommended by SERC.

Other power sources which are reasonable are: (1) nuclear power, (2) fossil steam, (3) simple cycle combustion turbines, (4) combined cycle combustion turbines, (5) conventional hydroelectric power, and (6) pumped storage hydroelectric power.

environmental_impact.text: Construction would clear about 505 acres of vegetation and wildlife habitat, including 370 acres of mixed forest within the impoundment area, and would eliminate approximately 2.3 miles of trout stream — about 1% of the state's trout streams. Howard Creek would experience a 53% flow reduction immediately below its confluence with Bad Creek, and at least 3.5 miles of the creek would be unsuitable for trout for years due to siltation, with destruction of approximately 1 mile of spawning habitat. Operation in combination with the Jocassee project is expected to reduce or eliminate optimum coldwater trout habitat in Lake Jocassee, threatening its two-story trout fishery, with fish entrainment mortality of 35-75% measured during turbine passage. Rare and endangered species including the green salamander and Oconee bells could be affected, and air quality and noise would be temporarily degraded by burning, equipment, and blasting.

Noise levels would be expected to increase during construction due to blasting, machinery operation, and other related construction procedures.

public_response.text: Public response was mixed: the Mayor of Walhalla endorsed the project and the Nuclear Regulatory Commission praised the alternatives section as extremely well written, while the South Carolina Wildlife and Marine Resources Department formally opposed the project and Trout Unlimited noted the state's trout streams are limited to about 250 miles. The Department of the Interior could not fully endorse the project until adverse impacts are mitigated, and EPA assigned an ER-2 rating (environmental reservations / insufficient information). The Joseph LeConte Chapter of the Sierra Club opposed the project, arguing it would waste 1.3 million MWh annually and that piecemeal development of multiple pumped-storage sites violates NEPA. Trout Unlimited requested public meetings and deferral of licensing pending completion of fishery studies, but Staff concluded it is not in the public interest to defer processing of the application.

themes.justification: The project centers on a 1,000-MW pumped storage facility powered by nuclear energy and connected via transmission lines (Energy Systems), while the environmental impacts prominently feature destruction of trout streams, coldwater fishery habitat in Lake Jocassee, and rare species like Oconee bells and green salamander (Wildlife and Natural Areas), and the project fundamentally alters water flows in Bad Creek, Howard Creek, and Lake Jocassee (Water Systems).
